issues.legal_issue: Removing the former share-allocation provision does not make the partition scheme arbitrary when equal per-member shares remain prescribed, and removing the power to exclude estate property from partition is reasonable.
material_facts: The amendment removed the former provision addressing members’ shares, while directing the Board to partition among those entitled to shares under the general family-property law, which provided for equal per-member shares.
The amendment also removed the Maharaja’s former power to exclude property from the partible estate.
The petitioner argued that these deletions left the Board free to determine shares and properties at its discretion.
issues.conclusion: The deletion of the former share provision was a drafting change that did not alter members’ substantive entitlement to equal shares; removing the power to exclude property was reasonable and beneficial to members.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14’s prohibition on arbitrary state action. It held that the general equal-share rule continued to govern, so the deleted provision was otiose, and that making all estate property available for partition avoided unjust exclusions.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_partition_am: A party challenges the constitutionality of legislation changing how a family estate is partitioned.
predicates.equal_per_member_shares_remain: The applicable rules continue to entitle each member to an equal individual share.
predicates.exclusion_power_removed: The amendment removes a decision-maker’s power to exclude property from the estate available for partition.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a partition amendment that preserves equal individual shares and removes a power to exclude estate property, the amendment does not make the partition scheme unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Using an established family board instead of civil courts to partition a very large and complex family estate is a reasonable alternative to ordinary partition litigation.
material_facts: The estate had around 800 members and included urban and rural lands, buildings, and other assets of considerable volume and value.
Ordinary partition litigation could involve prolonged proceedings, appeals, and related applications, delaying distribution and burdening members with limited resources.
The Board had managed the estate for decades, had previously been entrusted with partitioning it, and included senior members representing the family’s branches.
issues.conclusion: The non-court partition mechanism was reasonable in light of the circumstances and could not be condemned as discriminatory.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the arrangement under Article 14 in light of practical circumstances and distributive justice. It relied on the Board’s history and experience, and on the likely delay and hardship of ordinary civil partition proceedings, rather than treating access to a civil court as indispensable in every partition.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_partition_amendment and many_family_members and complex_estate_assets and prolonged_court_partition_likely and experienced_family_board_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_partition_am: A party challenges the constitutionality of legislation changing how a family estate is partitioned.
predicates.many_family_members: The estate is to be divided among a very large number of family members.
predicates.complex_estate_assets: The estate contains numerous or varied assets that make division by metes and bounds difficult.
predicates.prolonged_court_partition_likely: Ordinary court proceedings for partition are likely to take so long that distribution would be substantially delayed.
predicates.experienced_family_board_available: An established board with experience managing the estate and knowledge of the family is available to carry out the partition.

issues.definition: Where a constitutional challenge concerns partition among many members of a complex estate, prolonged court litigation is likely, and an experienced family board is available, using the board instead of civil courts is reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory board’s authority to partition family property is not unbridled when its rights-affecting function carries quasi-judicial duties and its conduct remains reviewable in writ proceedings.
material_facts: The amendment entrusted the existing statutory Board with partitioning the estate and made the resulting partition valid.
The Board was a longstanding body whose members included senior representatives of the family’s branches.
The Board’s partition decisions would affect members’ rights, and its actions remained subject to constitutional writ review.
issues.conclusion: The Board’s power was not unbridled or unconstitutional because the statute implied quasi-judicial responsibilities and its deviations could be reviewed under Article 226.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and held that a statutory body determining rights must act quasi-judicially. It relied on the availability of review under Article 226 and on the principles of natural justice discussed in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, M. S. Gill v. Union of India, and Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_partition_am: A party challenges the constitutionality of legislation changing how a family estate is partitioned.
predicates.statutory_board_determines_member_rights: A board created or continued by statute is assigned to decide matters that affect members’ rights.
predicates.writ_review_available: The board’s departures from legal requirements or arbitrary or bad-faith conduct can be challenged through constitutional writ proceedings.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a statutory board that determines members’ rights and remains subject to writ review, its partition power is not unbridled.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory board partitioning property while determining members’ rights must provide the fairness and procedural opportunities required of a quasi-judicial body.
material_facts: The Board was assigned to partition property and thereby determine the rights of family members.
The petitioner argued that the statute did not expressly require a hearing and could permit a secret or unfair process.
The Court directed that affected parties receive natural justice, reasons for conclusions, opportunities to address valuations and reports, and other reasonable procedural facilities.
issues.conclusion: The Board must act quasi-judicially and provide the procedural fairness and opportunities appropriate to determining members’ rights; its decisions remain reviewable for non-compliance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated quasi-judicial duties and natural justice as implied in the Board’s statutory function. It relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and M. S. Gill v. Union of India on natural justice, and Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India on reasons and procedural fairness in quasi-judicial proceedings.

predicates.statutory_board_partition_proceeding: A statutory board is conducting a proceeding to divide and allot family property.
predicates.board_determines_member_rights: The board’s decisions in the proceeding affect the rights or interests of persons entitled to shares.

issues.definition: When a statutory board partitions property in a proceeding that determines members’ rights, it must provide quasi-judicial fairness.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an appeal from a statutory board’s partition does not by itself make the partition scheme arbitrary when constitutional writ review remains available.
material_facts: The amendment did not provide an appeal from the partition effected by the Board.
The Board was a statutory body required to comply with the law and act quasi-judicially.
Members could seek constitutional writ review if the Board acted arbitrarily, in bad faith, or contrary to legal requirements.
issues.conclusion: The absence of an appeal did not make the scheme arbitrary because writ review under Article 226 provided a corrective remedy.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that absence of a right of appeal does not itself establish arbitrariness, relying on Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India. It also relied on the availability of constitutional review under Article 226 for unlawful, arbitrary, or bad-faith conduct by the statutory Board.

predicates.challenge_to_partition_scheme: A party challenges the legality or constitutionality of a scheme for partitioning family property.
predicates.no_appeal_from_board_partition: The scheme provides no appeal from the board’s partition decision.
predicates.writ_review_available: A person affected by unlawful, arbitrary, or bad-faith conduct can seek constitutional writ review.

issues.definition: When a partition scheme is challenged, it provides no appeal, and writ review remains available, the absence of an appeal does not make the scheme arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation providing a distinct partition procedure for a uniquely situated family estate is not impermissible class legislation when the special circumstances justify the difference in procedure.
material_facts: The legislation singled out a royal family estate for partition through a Board rather than through a civil court.
The family estate had a very large number of members and substantial, varied assets, making ordinary court partition especially burdensome and slow.
The substantive approach to shares was aligned with the rules applicable to other families, while the principal difference was the body carrying out the partition.
issues.conclusion: The legislation was a reasonable equalising measure, not hostile class legislation, because the special circumstances justified using a Board instead of a civil court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14’s equality principle and distinguished reasonable classification from hostile class legislation. It held that the estate’s distinctive circumstances justified the procedural difference while the substantive principles of partition remained similar to those governing other families.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_special_partition_law and distinctive_estate_circumstances and substantially_equal_share_principles and justified_procedural_difference

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_part: A party challenges legislation that establishes a distinct procedure for partitioning a particular family estate.
predicates.distinctive_estate_circumstances: The estate has circumstances, such as an unusually large number of members or complex assets, that distinguish it from ordinary family estates.
predicates.substantially_equal_share_principles: The substantive principles governing members’ shares are substantially similar to those applied to other comparable families.
predicates.justified_procedural_difference: The distinctive circumstances provide a reason for using a different body or procedure to carry out the partition.

issues.definition: When a special partition law addresses a distinctive estate, retains substantially equal share principles, and uses a procedure justified by those circumstances, its classification is not hostile.
